chunk_a.text_snippet:
Title: Children need protecting from social media – and generative AI
Date: 2026-01-22

Content: Politicians, parents and educators have got to help children to find and maintain real, deep connections in an analogue world. This doesn’t mean locking away all technology; it means regulating access to addictive and dangerous platforms at the peak of adolescent neuroplasticity and vulnerability. The answers are not new – sport, music, the rejuvenation of the youth club, simple role‑modelling – but those in power have got to take bold action to prevent the harms of social media being baked in for the next generation. Alexandra Cocksworth Deputy head, Lord Wandsworth College, Hampshire • Recent articles on the growing calls for a social media ban or greater restrictions rightly highlight that we are at a tipping point in this debate. In 2015, the Youth Sport Trust published the first of a trilogy of reports warning of a generation being held hostage by handheld devices. They’re connected 24/7, but lonelier than ever.

chunk_b.text_snippet:
Title: Britain facing ‘catastrophe’ because of children being addicted to social media, peers told – as it happened
Date: 2026-01-21

Content: Currently, many if not most social media companies have no really effective age assurance at 13. Thirdly, the amendment would direct the chief medical officer to prepare and publish advice to parents and carers on the use of social media by children. Fourthly, the amendment sends a message that draws a line in the sand for parents, carers and others to use when discussing social media with children which they are crying out for. And fifthly, it allows 12 months for implementation. In the House of Lords peers are just starting the debate covering the amendment to the children’s wellbeing and schools bill that would ban children under the age of 16 from having a social media account. The amendment has been tabled by Lord Nash, a Tory former education minister, but another signatory of the amendment is Hilary Cass, the crossbencher and paediatrician who compiled a landmark report on transgender services for young people. Nash’s amendment is number 94A.

initial_question.question: How does the proposed legislative change regarding social media access for children, as discussed in the House of Lords on 2026-01-21, align with the specific concerns raised by educators on 2026-01-22 regarding the need for regulatory intervention during adolescence?
initial_question.answer: The proposed amendment (number 94A) to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill, debated on 2026-01-21, seeks to ban children under 16 from having social media accounts to address concerns about platform addiction and ineffective age assurance. This aligns with the perspective presented by educators on 2026-01-22, who argue that bold regulatory action is necessary to protect adolescents from the harms of social media at the peak of their neuroplasticity and vulnerability, supporting the view that we are at a tipping point requiring such interventions.
